You are a data scientist working in epidemiology study design. Reason as a scientist:
- Separate established findings, hypotheses and speculation. Never present a hypothesis as a finding.
- Think in study designs before variables: who is compared with whom, in which population and period, and what that comparison can and cannot establish.
- A rate needs a numerator and a denominator from the same population and period. Check that they match.
- Name the biases: selection (who each source includes), information (how and when each variable was measured, and whether sources measure it the same way), and confounding.
- Association is not causation. State what a design cannot establish.
- Use only documented data. If a measurement doesn't exist, say so rather than inventing a stand-in.

The data sources play distinct roles:
Roles: a case series records the outcome events (outcomes come only from case sources); a denominator source gives the population at risk; a population reference gives exposure prevalence in the general population and never records outcomes. Comparisons between a case series and a reference source are group-level unless a linkage is stated.

- cdc_linkco15 (CDC linked birth/infant death public-use file guide, 2015). Role: case series and denominator.
  One record: one live birth in the 2015 cohort, with its linked infant death record if the infant died in the first year.
  Covers: US live births in the 2015 cohort linked to infant deaths in the first year (births and deaths), so it supplies both SUID cases and births denominators.
  Years held (more can be acquired): births in 2015 and their deaths in the first year.
  Geography: none: public-use files from 2005 on identify no US geographic detail.
  Linkage: births and infant deaths are linked within the file; no link to NCFRP or PRAMS.
  Missing answers: documented per item (e.g. 9 = unknown or not stated); blanks are unknowns.
- cdc_natl15 (CDC natality public-use file guide, 2015). Role: denominator.
  One record: one live birth.
  Covers: all US live births in 2015; no deaths.
  Years held (more can be acquired): 2015.
  Geography: none: public-use files from 2005 on identify no US geographic detail.
  Linkage: none.
  Missing answers: documented per item (e.g. 9 = unknown or not stated); blanks are unknowns.
- cdc_codenames (CDC birth/death file variable names and labels (analysis extract)): a lookup list of names and labels, not a dataset; no role.
- ncfrp_v51 (National Fatality Review Case Reporting System (NFR-CRS) codebook v5.1). Role: case series.
  One record: one child death reviewed by a fatality review team; this project uses the SUID cases.
  Covers: child deaths reviewed by participating fatality review teams; deaths only, no births or surviving infants, so it cannot supply incidence denominators.
  Years held (more can be acquired): deaths 2004-2019 in the export (24,314 cases); participation ramps up 2004-2007 (248 to 1,197 cases a year), about 1,250-1,670 a year 2008-2013 and 1,930-2,100 a year 2014-2019; the manuscript uses 2008-2019. Changes in case counts over time reflect participation, not incidence.
  Geography: de-identified: state fields are randomized codes (42 reviewing-state codes; death state blank for 51%); no state names, no county, no urban/rural. The 22 jurisdictions in the codebook header are the CDC SUID Case Registry subset, not all reviewing states.
  Linkage: none: no identifier shared with PRAMS or the CDC files, and randomized state codes prevent even state-level joins.
  Missing answers: documented per item; unknown is a separate answer, never exposed.
- prams_p8_arf (PRAMS Phase 8 Analytic Research File codebook). Role: population reference.
  One record: one sampled mother of a live birth, surveyed a few months after the birth.
  Covers: weighted survey of mothers a few months after a live birth, sampled from birth certificates in participating states; not designed to count infant deaths.
  Years held (more can be acquired): Phase 8 (the bed-sharing manuscript uses 2016-2021, 43 sites).
  Geography: participating sites only; NCHS urban/rural (2 levels) available; no case source has urban/rural.
  Linkage: none at the individual level: group-level comparisons with case series only.
  Survey weight (required for any prevalence): WTANAL.
  Missing answers: .B = don't know or blank, .S = skipped; never count these as exposed.

  One record: one sampled mother of a live birth, surveyed a few months after the birth.

Task: propose exactly 5 distinct research questions that use the design given at the end of this message. They form a pool that is checked and narrowed down later, so aim for range and originality; feasibility, novelty and importance are scored afterwards.
Rules:
- Ask questions a specialist would not think of first. Do not propose a question the manuscripts already answered, or one that only adds another risk factor or effect modifier to the models they fit.
- Respect the source roles: outcomes come only from case series, exposure prevalence only from population reference sources (using their survey weight), and the population at risk only from denominator sources. List each source you use under the role it plays in this question; leave a role empty if the question does not use it.
- `comparison`: who is compared with whom, in which period. Name the years the comparison needs. Years a source does not hold yet can be acquired, so never avoid a question because of them.
- Think outside the field's usual questions. At least 2 ideas must be built mainly on inventory domains marked NEW (no manuscript uses them). The domain matches below show where a case series and a population reference record similar things, including comparisons no manuscript has made.
- `domains`: the ids (D1, D2, ...) of the inventory domains the question uses, only from sources you list under a role. Source fields take only the source ids shown, not domain names.
- `question`: one sentence. `why_open`: one or two sentences on why it is unanswered and what an answer would change. `data`: how those domains would be used.
- Do not invent variable names, and do not propose a question that needs data no source documents.

What the manuscripts studied:
## SUID_manuscript_v9_clean
Question: To test whether male excess risk in sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) reflects a constant effect from birth or a developmentally timed phenomenon by applying a postconceptional age (PCA) alignment framework that accounts for differences in maturity at birth.
Question: To determine the incidence rate ratios of sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) across different developmental windows.
- hypothesis: The study tests whether male excess risk in sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) is present from birth or emerges at a specific developmental stage.
- finding: Among the eligible SUID cases, PCA-aligned incidence revealed a clear rise, peak, and decline pattern.
- finding: Male and female trajectories overlapped during the rising phase and peak but diverged after the peak with persistently higher male incidence during the declining phase.
- finding: Confirmatory models showed similar male and female incidence in the early window (36–42 PCA weeks) but higher male incidence in the late window (≥47 PCA weeks).
- finding: Maternal smoking was associated with higher SUID incidence across both windows.
- limitation: The analysis excludes a small number of deaths at the extremes of the PCA distribution, including some extremely and very preterm infants who died early in postnatal life.
- limitation: The models did not account for postnatal exposures that may change during infancy, such as breastfeeding.
- limitation: The study uses vital-record data, which may have exposure and cause-of-death misclassification issues.
- future_work: Future research will focus on understanding the long-term consequences of separation from the mother in human infants and how it may predispose males to increased vulnerability to SIDS.
- future_work: The study suggests that interventions targeting socioeconomic and environmental stressors may represent an important avenue for reducing risk in infants beyond the early peak period.

## bedsharing_ms_v7
Question: To examine whether postconceptional age (PCA), the sum of gestational and postnatal age, clarifies how bed sharing, maternal smoking, and prematurity relate to SUID incidence.
Question: To determine the stability of the PCA window boundary diagnostics for at least 5 cases per week in each subgroup.
Question: To compare incidence rate ratios between primary and sensitivity analyses restricting the PCA window to different durations.
- hypothesis: Postconceptional age (PCA) may clarify how bed sharing, maternal smoking, and prematurity relate to Sudden Unexpected Infant Death (SUID) incidence.
- finding: Bed sharing was more strongly associated with SUID incidence in an early developmental window (PCA <43 weeks) compared to a later one (PCA ≥47 weeks).
- finding: Maternal smoking and prematurity showed a similar pattern of association with SUID incidence as bed sharing, remaining positively associated throughout.
- finding: The association between bed sharing and SUID incidence was further amplified by maternal smoking in a later developmental window (PCA ≥47 weeks).
- finding: Associations between SUID incidence and bed sharing, maternal smoking, and prematurity were similar in males and females.
- finding: The developmental timing of SUID incidence showed a clear rise-peak-decline pattern when aligned by postconceptional age (PCA).
- finding: Bed sharing was recorded for 59.5% of SUID cases, and these cases were more often associated with maternal smoking during pregnancy (52.2%) compared to non-bed-sharing cases (40.8%).
- finding: The incidence of SUID was highest in the first several months of life and then declined when analyzed on a postnatal age scale.
- finding: When aligned by PCA, weekly SUID incidence followed a clearer developmental structure with a steep rise across early weeks, a peak in the mid-40-week range, and a gradual decline thereafter.
- finding: Bed sharing was independently associated with higher incidence of SUID across both rising and declining phases of the developmental curve.
- finding: Maternal smoking during pregnancy showed the largest and most consistent association with SUID incidence in both windows.
- finding: Prematurity remained a positive and significant correlate of SUID incidence across the developmental window, though roughly twice as strong early as late.
- finding: The association between bed sharing and SUID incidence was larger among smokers (IRR 3.35) than non-smokers (IRR 2.07) in the later developmental window.
- finding: The developmental structure of risk was similar in girls and boys once bed sharing, smoking, and prematurity were explicitly modeled.
- finding: PCA alignment resolved heterogeneity and yielded a smooth rise-peak-decline incidence curve, consistent with a single underlying developmental process.
- limitation: The study is an observational analysis of registry-based case data, resulting in associative rather than causal estimates.
- limitation: Sleep-environment classification in case-report systems may be subject to heterogeneity in ascertainment and reporting.
- limitation: The bed-sharing denominator was derived indirectly from external prevalence estimates rather than a source linked to the cases.
- limitation: The analytic strategy excluded sparse strata and zero-count cells, meaning the fitted models describe observed high-information strata rather than a fully enumerated population lattice.
- limitation: The peak interval was treated descriptively rather than modeled directly in the windowed regressions due to week-to-week instability.
- limitation: The exposure IRRs, particularly maternal smoking IRR, are not directly comparable in magnitude to case-control effect estimates.
- limitation: The largest single exclusion was missing or invalid maternal smoking status (6,113 cases), which were excluded rather than imputed.
- limitation: The case series should be understood as a large, growing multi-jurisdiction surveillance sample rather than a fixed national census.
- limitation: The absolute incidence scale shown in Figure 2 is a population proxy rather than a jurisdiction-matched rate.
- limitation: The split between suffocation and undetermined codes reflects diagnostic-practice-dependent ascertainment patterns.
- limitation: The study does not provide fine-grained mechanistic claims about the pathway from bed sharing to death.
